> "Maze Avenger"
> By Dale Low
> ARCADIAN, 6, no. 11/12 (October 31, 1984): 100.
> Documentation by Adam Trionfo
>
> About "Maze Avenger"
> --------------------
>
> Note that the Arcadian newsletter provided no instructions on how to play this game.
>
> "Maze Avenger" is a maze game where the player's character creeps ever so slowly around the maze shooting objects that are not at all easily identifiable.  When the character shoots all of the objects on the screen then the player advances to the next level.  The player can be hit by-- well-- SOMETHING and it causes the player to be unable to shoot and also to be able to pass through walls.
>
>
> How to load "Maze Avenger"
> --------------------------
>
> In AstroBASIC type:
>
> :INPUT
>
> As the tape loads, on the screen will appear:
>
> >PRINT ";STOP";:PRINT %(16
> 384),1948
> ;STOP
>
> This is normal.  This is how the program has to be saved, otherwise the load ends with "WHAT?" (the STOP command prevents the error).  This format of saving does not seem to be compatible with my normal method of archiving a program by first clearing the screen and printing the game's title and author.  Therefore, the user gets to see the special method that had to be used to be save the game to tape so that both the BASIC program and data array would be preserved.
>
> After the game has loaded, type:
>
> RUN
>
> In AstroBASIC many games can be loaded and run at the same time by typing :INPUT ; RUN.  This method will NOT work for this game.
>
>
> Typing and Archiving "Maze Avenger"
> -----------------------------------
>
> Of course, "Maze Avenger" has already been typed and can be played right away.  This additional information is for archival purposes.  It may also be of use in the future when archiving a similar program that includes both a BASIC program and a data array.
>
> "Maze Avenger" has been one of the most difficult programs to archive properly.  Dozens of discussion group postings and emails, well over fifty of them, were exchanged between several people who worked to get this archived correctly back in March of 2011.  These people include Richard Degler, Ken Lill, Paul Thacker, Mike White and myself.  Normally archiving a program involves no exchanges of emails or postings except to announce that a program is ready to be added to BallyAlley.com.
>
> "Maze Avenger" does not work correctly as printed in the Arcadian.  For this reason, there are two versions of the program archived.  One version is archived as it is printed in the Arcadian.  This version is for archival purposes only and should be avoided.  The second version includes fixes made by Richard Degler so that the game runs correctly.
>
> The Arcadian provided only a BASIC listing of the program along with the ML program data array that is written separately into the Line Input Buffer.  The data array listing expects you to load each memory location separately.  This turns out to be a lot of typing.  Richard Degler suggested using a short direct command to enter the data.  Here is his (slightly modified) command that prompts the user for data for all twenty-one memory locations:
>
> FOR A=20237TO A+40STEP 2;PRINT A,;INPUT %(A);NEXT A
>
> Once the data array has been entered, check that it has been entered accurately with this direct command:
>
> FOR A=20237TO A+40STEP 2;PRINT A," = ",";PRINT %(A);NEXT A
>
> This command prints the memory location along with the value that the location holds.  Remember that you can hit the PAUSE key to pause the listing and then GO to continue.
>
> If you want to save the data array separately (for example, if you only type in part of the data array and you want to continue later), type:
>
> :PRINT %(20237),21
>
> This will save the twenty-one memory locations (and the extra one byte checksum that follows all tape saves).  To load the data array back into the proper location, type:
>
> :INPUT %(20237)
>
> This will load the data array beginning at memory location 20237.  The last byte of the data array will end in 20277.  Note that address 20279 will hold the one byte checksum that was stored on tape.
>
> This commands can each be slightly modified and used to save any data array.
>
> No additional information about what the program does were included in the Arcadian, although brief instructions for saving the program were included.  As printed, they are:
>
> "After entering the program and the data array PRINT the whole thing to tape like this:
>
> :PRINT %(16384),2000
>
> This will save your data [array and program] too."
>
> What the instructions don't mention about saving is that while this method of saving the program and data array does work, the user will always get a "WHAT?" when the program is loaded from tape.  To avoid this, use this syntax instead:
>
> PRINT ";STOP";:PRINT %(16384),2000
>
> Now when the program is loaded there is no "WHAT?" error, but the adverse affect is that the program can't include a title screen.
>
> For additional details about solving the "Maze Avenger" saving/loading problem, see this document:
>
> http://tinyurl.com/4x53sv8
>
> (or use the full URL:)
>
> http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/misc/Maze%20Avenger/Solving%20the%20Maze%20Avenger%20Saving%20and%20Loading%20Problem.txt
>
>
> The Disassembly
> ---------------
>
> Richard Degler disassembled the machine language portion of "Maze Avenger."  Normal, this would be of most use to assembly programs, but in this instance his disassembly also includes the complete BASIC program, which he commented in detail.  If you would like to know more about the program, then his disassembly is the place to look.  It can be found here:
>
> http://tinyurl.com/42js6tn
>
> (or use the full URL:)
>
> http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/misc/Maze%20Avenger/Maze%20Avenger.asm
>
>
> Was It Worth It?
> ----------------
>
> Not only was "Maze Avenger" difficult to archive, but the game turns out to be crude and without any much fun-factor that I can discern.  The game is B&W, it is impossible to tell what the enemies is or what the players is shooting and the character moves so slowly that it is painful to clear one level, let alone continue to play after that.  Perhaps there is an element of gameplay that I don't know about.  If you seem to have found the fun in this game, or if you found how to actually PLAY this game and can explain what is happening, then please let me know.
>
> Looking back at archiving this game, and accounting for the many hours that it took to finally get it right (including the time spent by Richard Degler tracking down and fixing the errors and also disassembling the machine language routines), was it worth the time?  Sure.  I learned more while archiving this Bally/Astrocade program then most any other and I'll be able to use this information in the future to archive more exciting software.
>
>
> For those that made it this far and read EVERYTHING (including the links), you are probably one of a king.
>
> Thanks again to everyone that helped to get this program archived.  There is just NO way I could have done it alone-- I would have given up ages ago!
>
> Finally, if anyone wants to figure this game out and create some gameplay information, then that would be awesome.  Even the most basic of information would be useful.
>
> Have fun!
>
> Adam

Paul wrote:
>>
I managed to reach level five and score 171 points.
>>

First off, unless you've played the "Maze Avenger," you have NO idea how hard Paul must have worked and how long he played to get that seemingly low score of 172.  I think my "high" score is in the twenties.  Paul should feel lucky to have scored from one level to the next, as that was one of the bugs that Richard fixed from the version printed in the Arcadian.

>>
I'm going to assume this is a world record unless someone claims otherwise.

>>

Oh, this sure made me laugh!  I bet, no, I DARE someone else to play this game long enough to beat that score.

>>
I figured I should play this game after all the trouble everyone went through archiving it.
>>

Thanks, I appreciate that.  I figure that somewhere, a bunch of different someones have played or used all of the games and programs on BallyAlley.com at one time or another, but this is the sort of thing that I wouldn't hear back about.  It would be neat to someday have an area on BallyAlley.com where people could leave comments on each program.

>>
It is pretty frustrating, but I have a few tips.
>>

I know that "Maze Avenger" doesn't have differently named individual sequences, but from the way you wrote about them, it sounds completely official.  Paul, it sounds like you have written the complete manual for the game.  If this is okay, then just say so and I'll include it in the game's archive.

>>
I'm not actually sure what the sprites are supposed to be
>>

In Richard's commented BASIC code, he calls these "sprites" fruits.  Both you and he have active imaginations.  To me they look like screwed-up graphics but they could just as well be transdimensional boxes that have only part of their matter in this dimension .  I thought that these graphics were part of the machine language routine, but only the player's character is included there.  Perhaps the fruit/treasure/alien druglords are drawn with the BOX command in one or more of the lines 6-15.  Richard comments this as "first Erase off-screen," but I'm not sure if he means the ENTIRE Box-drawing section.  It's interesting to note that these treasures look to be the same (or very similar) to those used in another of Dale's other games (either "Pac*Man" or "Control 30," I can't remember which one).

I'm not sure if I mentioned this before, but "Maze Avenger," for a BASIC game, draws the game mighty fast, which is a huge plus for a game that has the player move slowly.

Thanks for playing and commenting on the game, Paul.

Adam

> Forgive my indulgence, but this is going to be a rather long posting.  Some of this will be useful and interesting in general while some of it is specific to this program.  A bit of it is aimed most squarely at just trying to keep track of everything that it took to get this program archived.  Even the most general information, such as how to load and save the game, is different from other archived software (although it seems that Paul is getting in mighty deep with the programs that require extra RAM).  I hope that keeping this record will help with archiving efforts for this platform in the future.

>

>

> "Maze Avenger"

> By Dale Low

> ARCADIAN, 6, no. 11/12 (October 31, 1984): 100.

> Documentation by Adam Trionfo

>

> About "Maze Avenger"

> --------------------

>

> Note that the Arcadian newsletter provided no instructions on how to play this game.

>

> "Maze Avenger" is a maze game where the player's character creeps ever so slowly around the maze shooting objects that are not at all easily identifiable.  When the character shoots all of the objects on the screen then the player advances to the next level.  The player can be hit by-- well-- SOMETHING and it causes the player to be unable to shoot and also to be able to pass through walls.

>

>

> How to load "Maze Avenger"

> --------------------------

>

> In AstroBASIC type:

>

> :INPUT

>

> As the tape loads, on the screen will appear:

>

> >PRINT ";STOP";:PRINT %(16

> 384),1948

> ;STOP

>

> This is normal.  This is how the program has to be saved, otherwise the load ends with "WHAT?" (the STOP command prevents the error).  This format of saving does not seem to be compatible with my normal method of archiving a program by first clearing the screen and printing the game's title and author.  Therefore, the user gets to see the special method that had to be used to be save the game to tape so that both the BASIC program and data array would be preserved.

>

> After the game has loaded, type:

>

> RUN

>

> In AstroBASIC many games can be loaded and run at the same time by typing :INPUT ; RUN.  This method will NOT work for this game.

>

>

> Typing and Archiving "Maze Avenger"

> -----------------------------------

>

> Of course, "Maze Avenger" has already been typed and can be played right away.  This additional information is for archival purposes.  It may also be of use in the future when archiving a similar program that includes both a BASIC program and a data array.

>

> "Maze Avenger" has been one of the most difficult programs to archive properly.  Dozens of discussion group postings and emails, well over fifty of them, were exchanged between several people who worked to get this archived correctly back in March of 2011.  These people include Richard Degler, Ken Lill, Paul Thacker, Mike White and myself.  Normally archiving a program involves no exchanges of emails or postings except to announce that a program is ready to be added to BallyAlley.com.

>

> "Maze Avenger" does not work correctly as printed in the Arcadian.  For this reason, there are two versions of the program archived.  One version is archived as it is printed in the Arcadian.  This version is for archival purposes only and should be avoided.  The second version includes fixes made by Richard Degler so that the game runs correctly.

>

> The Arcadian provided only a BASIC listing of the program along with the ML program data array that is written separately into the Line Input Buffer.  The data array listing expects you to load each memory location separately.  This turns out to be a lot of typing.  Richard Degler suggested using a short direct command to enter the data.  Here is his (slightly modified) command that prompts the user for data for all twenty-one memory locations:

>

> FOR A=20237TO A+40STEP 2;PRINT A,;INPUT %(A);NEXT A

>

> Once the data array has been entered, check that it has been entered accurately with this direct command:

>

> FOR A=20237TO A+40STEP 2;PRINT A," = ",";PRINT %(A);NEXT A

>

> This command prints the memory location along with the value that the location holds.  Remember that you can hit the PAUSE key to pause the listing and then GO to continue.

>

> If you want to save the data array separately (for example, if you only type in part of the data array and you want to continue later), type:

>

> :PRINT %(20237),21

>

> This will save the twenty-one memory locations (and the extra one byte checksum that follows all tape saves).  To load the data array back into the proper location, type:

>

> :INPUT %(20237)

>

> This will load the data array beginning at memory location 20237.  The last byte of the data array will end in 20277.  Note that address 20279 will hold the one byte checksum that was stored on tape.

>

> This commands can each be slightly modified and used to save any data array.

>

> No additional information about what the program does were included in the Arcadian, although brief instructions for saving the program were included.  As printed, they are:

>

> "After entering the program and the data array PRINT the whole thing to tape like this:

>

> :PRINT %(16384),2000

>

> This will save your data [array and program] too."

>

> What the instructions don't mention about saving is that while this method of saving the program and data array does work, the user will always get a "WHAT?" when the program is loaded from tape.  To avoid this, use this syntax instead:

>

> PRINT ";STOP";:PRINT %(16384),2000

>

> Now when the program is loaded there is no "WHAT?" error, but the adverse affect is that the program can't include a title screen.

>

> For additional details about solving the "Maze Avenger" saving/loading problem, see this document:

>

> http://tinyurl.com/4x53sv8

>

> (or use the full URL:)

>

> http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/misc/Maze%20Avenger/Solving%20the%20Maze%20Avenger%20Saving%20and%20Loading%20Problem.txt

>

>

> The Disassembly

> ---------------

>

> Richard Degler disassembled the machine language portion of "Maze Avenger."  Normal, this would be of most use to assembly programs, but in this instance his disassembly also includes the complete BASIC program, which he commented in detail.  If you would like to know more about the program, then his disassembly is the place to look.  It can be found here:

>

> http://tinyurl.com/42js6tn

>

> (or use the full URL:)

>

> http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/misc/Maze%20Avenger/Maze%20Avenger.asm

>

>

> Was It Worth It?

> ----------------

>

> Not only was "Maze Avenger" difficult to archive, but the game turns out to be crude and without any much fun-factor that I can discern.  The game is B&W, it is impossible to tell what the enemies is or what the players is shooting and the character moves so slowly that it is painful to clear one level, let alone continue to play after that.  Perhaps there is an element of gameplay that I don't know about.  If you seem to have found the fun in this game, or if you found how to actually PLAY this game and can explain what is happening, then please let me know.

>

> Looking back at archiving this game, and accounting for the many hours that it took to finally get it right (including the time spent by Richard Degler tracking down and fixing the errors and also disassembling the machine language routines), was it worth the time?  Sure.  I learned more while archiving this Bally/Astrocade program then most any other and I'll be able to use this information in the future to archive more exciting software.

>

>

> For those that made it this far and read EVERYTHING (including the links), you are probably one of a king.

>

> Thanks again to everyone that helped to get this program archived.  There is just NO way I could have done it alone-- I would have given up ages ago!

>

> Finally, if anyone wants to figure this game out and create some gameplay information, then that would be awesome.  Even the most basic of information would be useful.

>

> Have fun!

>

> Adam

>

11380:
I added "Cartridge Tester" by Ken Lill to BallyAlley.com.  This cartridge tester is used to test newly-created Bally/Astrocade cartridges.  This program requires expanded memory to run.

"Cartridge Tester" can be downloaded here:


http://tinyurl.com/3oaho7q

(or use the full URL:)

http://www.ballyalley.com/emulation/cart_images/cart_images/Cartridge%20Tester/Cartridge%20Tester%20(Ken%20Lill).zip


Here are the full details of the program:


Cartridge Tester
By Ken Lill
Directions, October 26, 2011
By Ken Lill and Adam Trionfo
----------------------------

This cartridge tester is used to test newly-created Bally/Astrocade cartridges.

These instructions are skeletal at best.  It is presumed that the user has plenty of knowledge on the use of extended memory as well as the traditional cartridge-swapping technique.

This an in-house program written by Ken Lill to test the creation of the homebrew "Crazy Climber" cartridges.  It compares a program in extended memory with an 8K program in cartridge area ($2000-$3FFF).

Here are the brief instructions from the assembly file:


;  Tester (Final)
;  By Ken Lill
;  June 21, 2011
;  Version 1.0
;
;  Assembled by hand by Ken Lill.
;
;  Compares cart using Bally/Astrocade and RAM expansion unit.
;
;  Version 1.0 - June 21, 2011 - Ken Lill
;     - Programmed by Ken Lill, and disassembled from original
;       ROM file using DZ80 2.0 and Richard Degler's BallyHVG.LUA
;       script by Adam Trionfo.
;     - Put into ZMac assembler format from disassembled file with
;       lots of hand disassembly.
;     - Comments added by Adam Trionfo based on information relayed
;       via telephone to Adam.
;     - This program assembles into the EXACT bytes that were in the
;       original file.  However, the binary file must be edited by
;       hand to get all of the bytes in the correct order and to remove
;       the extra zeros that are created from $2000-$6000. 
;   
;  This code can be assembled into a usable binary using the ZMac
;  assembler.  Here is a sample of the command line required:
;
;      zmac -i -m -o tester2.bin -x tester2.lst tester2.asm        


Here is the initial email that Ken sent along with version one of the program
(which was only a binary file).


Subject: Special Tester
From:    kenn lill
Sent:    Tue 6/21/11 10:36 AM
To:      Adam Trionfo

I have finally finished the cart tester. To use this tester, first burn a chip. any size will do, as there are only $121 bytes total!

Next, take the utility (LWR - either one) and put a known good database into $8000 of the Lil' WHITE RAM (or blue ram).

Then just insert the new cart. the screen will tell you what to do. This is the best way to test a cart thoroughly. It  will tell you if it's good or not. If it is bad, mark down the data on the screen and tape it to the cart. Return it to me for a new one.

The whole process takes less than a second to test each cart.

I hope this will make double checking much easier on your end. This program is expecting an 8K cart. Any more and it won't be able to test it. Any less, and the 1st address after the end will show up bad.


This program copies the "Cartridge Tester" program into extended memory and then runs.  Cartridges are switched in and out with the power on as needed.  If you have trouble (as I do) switching cartridges while your Astrocade is on, then this program will NOT work for you.


Note that this program will run in the MESS emulator if expanded memory is being used.  However, since cartridge can't be switched out, the program can not be used as it can on real hardware.


If you just scratched your head and wonder what THAT was all about, then I don't blame you.  Unless you are creating your own cartridges for this system, then you will have no use for this program at all.  If you ARE creating cartridges, then "Cartridge Tester" would prove a valuable utility to have in your Astrocade arsenal of software.

Thanks for the program, Ken-- and I really enjoyed creating the assembly source with you.

Have fun!

Adam

> So I figured I should play this game after all the trouble

> frustrating, but I have a few tips. The game alternates
> between a hunting sequence and a chase sequence. During the
> hunting sequence, your character walks very slowly and can't
> go through walls, but is able to fire his weapon. The weapon
> fires in the direction you're walking and keeps going until
> it hits a wall or one of the garbled sprites. I'm not
> actually sure what the sprites are supposed to be – maybe
> they're treasure you're shooting with your teleporter beam,
> maybe they're alien druglords that killed your family – we
> may never know. You can't walk while it's firing, so don't
> fire frivolously. Here's a hint to speed up the hunt. If
> you're standing right next to a wall, you can shoot through
> it. I'm not sure if this is actually intentional, but it's
> certainly useful. You score a few points for each object you
> shoot, and you reach the next level once you've gotten them
> all, at which point you get a bonus score and the maze
> resets with more objects.
>
> But you didn't think you could get through this maze
> unavenged, did you? Periodically we switch to the chase
> sequence. Now your weapon is of no use, and you can only
> flee in terror before the flashing block of death. You're so
> frightened, in fact, that you move much more quickly and you
> can run right through those walls. Stay away for a few
> seconds and you'll survive. Otherwise it will take a shot at
> you and you'll be instantly killed if it hits. Of course, if
> the block appears right next to you, you're pretty much
> screwed. On the plus side, you can take advantage of this
> phase to position yourself closer to your quarry.
>
> I managed to reach level five and score 171 points. I'm
> going to assume this is a world record unless someone claims
> otherwise.

>       So I figured I should play this game
> after all the trouble everyone went through archiving
> it.  It is pretty frustrating, but I have a few tips.
> The game alternates between a hunting sequence and a chase
> sequence. During the hunting sequence, your character walks
> very slowly and can't go through walls, but is able to fire
> his weapon. The weapon fires in the direction you're walking
> and keeps going until it hits a wall or one of the garbled
> sprites. I'm not actually sure what the sprites are supposed
> to be – maybe they're treasure you're shooting with your
> teleporter beam, maybe they're alien druglords that killed
> your family – we may never know. You can't walk while it's
> firing, so don't fire frivolously. Here's a hint to speed up
> the hunt. If you're standing right next to a wall, you can
> shoot through it. I'm not sure if this is actually
> intentional, but it's certainly useful. You score a few
> points for each object you shoot, and you reach the next
> level once you've gotten them all, at which point you get a
> bonus score and the maze resets with more objects.
>
>
>
> But you didn't think you could get through this maze
> unavenged, did you? Periodically we switch to the chase
> sequence. Now your weapon is of no use, and you can only
> flee in terror before the flashing block of death. You're so
> frightened, in fact, that you move much more quickly and you
> can run right through those walls. Stay away for a few
> seconds and you'll survive. Otherwise it will take a shot at
> you and you'll be instantly killed if it hits. Of course, if
> the block appears right next to you, you're pretty much
> screwed. On the plus side, you can take advantage of this
> phase to position yourself closer to your quarry. 
>
>
>
> I managed to reach level five and score 171 points. I'm
> going to assume this is a world record unless someone claims
> otherwise.
>
>
>
> Paul

>
> > --------------------
>

>
> > Note that the Arcadian newsletter provided no
> instructions on how to play this game.
>
> >
>
> > "Maze Avenger" is a maze game where the player's
> character creeps ever so slowly around the maze shooting
> objects that are not at all easily identifiable.  When the
> character shoots all of the objects on the screen then the
> player advances to the next level.  The player can be hit
> by-- well-- SOMETHING and it causes the player to be unable
> to shoot and also to be able to pass through walls.
>
> >
>
> >
>
> > How to load "Maze Avenger"
>
> > --------------------------
>
> >
>
> > In AstroBASIC type:
>
> >
>
> > :INPUT
>
> >
>
> > As the tape loads, on the screen will appear:
>
> >
>
> > >PRINT ";STOP";:PRINT %(16
>
> > 384),1948
>
> > ;STOP
>
> >
>
> > This is normal.  This is how the program has to be
> saved, otherwise the load ends with "WHAT?" (the STOP
> command prevents the error).  This format of saving does
> not seem to be compatible with my normal method of archiving
> a program by first clearing the screen and printing the
> game's title and author.  Therefore, the user gets to see
> the special method that had to be used to be save the game
> to tape so that both the BASIC program and data array would
> be preserved.
>
> >
>
> > After the game has loaded, type:
>
> >
>
> > RUN
>
> >
>
> > In AstroBASIC many games can be loaded and run at the
> same time by typing :INPUT ; RUN.  This method will NOT
> work for this game.
>
> >
>
> >
>
> > Typing and Archiving "Maze Avenger"
>
> > -----------------------------------
>
> >
>
> > Of course, "Maze Avenger" has already been typed and
> can be played right away.  This additional information is
> for archival purposes.  It may also be of use in the future
> when archiving a similar program that includes both a BASIC
> program and a data array.

>

> programs to archive properly.  Dozens of discussion group
> postings and emails, well over fifty of them, were exchanged
> between several people who worked to get this archived
> correctly back in March of 2011.  These people include
> Richard Degler, Ken Lill, Paul Thacker, Mike White and

> So I figured I should play this game after all the trouble
> everyone went through archiving it. It is pretty
> frustrating, but I have a few tips. The game alternates
> between a hunting sequence and a chase sequence. During the
> hunting sequence, your character walks very slowly and can't
> go through walls, but is able to fire his weapon. The weapon
> fires in the direction you're walking and keeps going until
> it hits a wall or one of the garbled sprites. I'm not
> actually sure what the sprites are supposed to be – maybe
> they're treasure you're shooting with your teleporter beam,
> maybe they're alien druglords that killed your family – we
> may never know. You can't walk while it's firing, so don't
> fire frivolously. Here's a hint to speed up the hunt. If
> you're standing right next to a wall, you can shoot through
> it. I'm not sure if this is actually intentional, but it's
> certainly useful. You score a few points for each object you
> shoot, and you reach the next level once you've gotten them
> all, at which point you get a bonus score and the maze
> resets with more objects.
>
> But you didn't think you could get through this maze
> unavenged, did you? Periodically we switch to the chase
> sequence. Now your weapon is of no use, and you can only
> flee in terror before the flashing block of death. You're so
> frightened, in fact, that you move much more quickly and you
> can run right through those walls. Stay away for a few
> seconds and you'll survive. Otherwise it will take a shot at
> you and you'll be instantly killed if it hits. Of course, if
> the block appears right next to you, you're pretty much
> screwed. On the plus side, you can take advantage of this
> phase to position yourself closer to your quarry.
>
> I managed to reach level five and score 171 points. I'm
> going to assume this is a world record unless someone claims
> otherwise.
>
> Paul

> > "Maze Avenger"
> > By Dale Low
> > ARCADIAN, 6, no. 11/12 (October 31, 1984): 100.
> > Documentation by Adam Trionfo
> >
> > About "Maze Avenger"
> > --------------------
> >
> > Note that the Arcadian newsletter provided no
> instructions on how to play this game.
> >
> > "Maze Avenger" is a maze game where the player's
> character creeps ever so slowly around the maze shooting
> objects that are not at all easily identifiable.  When the
> character shoots all of the objects on the screen then the
> player advances to the next level.  The player can be hit
> by-- well-- SOMETHING and it causes the player to be unable
> to shoot and also to be able to pass through walls.
> >
> >
> > How to load "Maze Avenger"
> > --------------------------
> >
> > In AstroBASIC type:
> >
> > :INPUT
> >
> > As the tape loads, on the screen will appear:
> >
> > >PRINT ";STOP";:PRINT %(16
> > 384),1948
> > ;STOP
> >
> > This is normal.  This is how the program has to be
> saved, otherwise the load ends with "WHAT?" (the STOP
> command prevents the error).  This format of saving does
> not seem to be compatible with my normal method of archiving
> a program by first clearing the screen and printing the
> game's title and author.  Therefore, the user gets to see
> the special method that had to be used to be save the game
> to tape so that both the BASIC program and data array would
> be preserved.
> >
> > After the game has loaded, type:
> >
> > RUN
> >
> > In AstroBASIC many games can be loaded and run at the
> same time by typing :INPUT ; RUN.  This method will NOT
> work for this game.
> >
> >
> > Typing and Archiving "Maze Avenger"
> > -----------------------------------
> >
> > Of course, "Maze Avenger" has already been typed and
> can be played right away.  This additional information is
> for archival purposes.  It may also be of use in the future
> when archiving a similar program that includes both a BASIC
> program and a data array.
> >
> > "Maze Avenger" has been one of the most difficult
> programs to archive properly.  Dozens of discussion group
> postings and emails, well over fifty of them, were exchanged
> between several people who worked to get this archived
> correctly back in March of 2011.  These people include
> Richard Degler, Ken Lill, Paul Thacker, Mike White and
> myself.  Normally archiving a program involves no exchanges
> of emails or postings except to announce that a program is
> ready to be added to BallyAlley.com.
> >
> > "Maze Avenger" does not work correctly as printed in
> the Arcadian.  For this reason, there are two versions of
> the program archived.  One version is archived as it is
> printed in the Arcadian.  This version is for archival
> purposes only and should be avoided.  The second version
> includes fixes made by Richard Degler so that the game runs
> correctly.
> >
> > The Arcadian provided only a BASIC listing of the
> program along with the ML program data array that is written
> separately into the Line Input Buffer.  The data array
> listing expects you to load each memory location
> separately.  This turns out to be a lot of typing.
> Richard Degler suggested using a short direct command to
> enter the data.  Here is his (slightly modified) command
> that prompts the user for data for all twenty-one memory
> locations:
> >
> > FOR A=20237TO A+40STEP 2;PRINT A,;INPUT %(A);NEXT A
> >
> > Once the data array has been entered, check that it
> has been entered accurately with this direct command:
> >
> > FOR A=20237TO A+40STEP 2;PRINT A," = ",";PRINT
> %(A);NEXT A
> >
> > This command prints the memory location along with the
> value that the location holds.  Remember that you can hit
> the PAUSE key to pause the listing and then GO to continue.
> >
> > If you want to save the data array separately (for
> example, if you only type in part of the data array and you
> want to continue later), type:
> >
> > :PRINT %(20237),21
> >
> > This will save the twenty-one memory locations (and
> the extra one byte checksum that follows all tape saves).
> To load the data array back into the proper location, type:
> >
> > :INPUT %(20237)
> >
> > This will load the data array beginning at memory
> location 20237.  The last byte of the data array will end
> in 20277.  Note that address 20279 will hold the one byte
> checksum that was stored on tape.
> >
> > This commands can each be slightly modified and used
> to save any data array.
> >
> > No additional information about what the program does
> were included in the Arcadian, although brief instructions
> for saving the program were included.  As printed, they
> are:
> >
> > "After entering the program and the data array PRINT
> the whole thing to tape like this:
> >
> > :PRINT %(16384),2000
> >
> > This will save your data [array and program] too."
> >
> > What the instructions don't mention about saving is
> that while this method of saving the program and data array
> does work, the user will always get a "WHAT?" when the
> program is loaded from tape.  To avoid this, use this
> syntax instead:
> >
> > PRINT ";STOP";:PRINT %(16384),2000
> >
> > Now when the program is loaded there is no "WHAT?"
> error, but the adverse affect is that the program can't
> include a title screen.
> >
> > For additional details about solving the "Maze
> Avenger" saving/loading problem, see this document:
> >
> > http://tinyurl.com/4x53sv8
> >
> > (or use the full URL:)
> >
> > http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/misc/Maze%20Avenger/Solving%20the%20Maze%20Avenger%20Saving%20and%20Loading%20Problem.txt
> >
> >
> > The Disassembly
> > ---------------
> >
> > Richard Degler disassembled the machine language
> portion of "Maze Avenger."  Normal, this would be of most
> use to assembly programs, but in this instance his
> disassembly also includes the complete BASIC program, which
> he commented in detail.  If you would like to know more
> about the program, then his disassembly is the place to
> look.  It can be found here:
> >
> > http://tinyurl.com/42js6tn
> >
> > (or use the full URL:)
> >
> > http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/misc/Maze%20Avenger/Maze%20Avenger.asm
> >
> >
> > Was It Worth It?
> > ----------------
> >
> > Not only was "Maze Avenger" difficult to archive, but
> the game turns out to be crude and without any much
> fun-factor that I can discern.  The game is B&W, it is
> impossible to tell what the enemies is or what the players
> is shooting and the character moves so slowly that it is
> painful to clear one level, let alone continue to play after
> that.  Perhaps there is an element of gameplay that I don't
> know about.  If you seem to have found the fun in this
> game, or if you found how to actually PLAY this game and can
> explain what is happening, then please let me know.
> >
> > Looking back at archiving this game, and accounting
> for the many hours that it took to finally get it right
> (including the time spent by Richard Degler tracking down
> and fixing the errors and also disassembling the machine
> language routines), was it worth the time?  Sure.  I
> learned more while archiving this Bally/Astrocade program
> then most any other and I'll be able to use this information
> in the future to archive more exciting software.
> >
> >
> > For those that made it this far and read EVERYTHING
> (including the links), you are probably one of a king.
> >
> > Thanks again to everyone that helped to get this
> program archived.  There is just NO way I could have done
> it alone-- I would have given up ages ago!
> >
> > Finally, if anyone wants to figure this game out and
> create some gameplay information, then that would be
> awesome.  Even the most basic of information would be
> useful.
> >
> > Have fun!
> >
> > Adam
>

I'm working my way through testing Richard's BASICart conversions on real hardware.  All of these carts are 8K ROMs.  I'm burning them to EPROM, and I'm (re)learning the hard way that EPROMs are temperamental beasts.  I'm using 2764s, which are 8K.  These were made about thirty years ago.  Even though they are new old-stock, they are LONG past their life expectancy.  It is a project in itself just to get good burns of software so that I can test it on my cart.

I've been contacting Richard with comments about the programs via email which is working well.  He removed some of the programs that were once available in the discussion group's file area.  These three programs were removed for copyright reasons:

1) "Life" By Jay Fenton
2) "Nuke the Bastards" By Jay Fenton
3) "Meteoroids" By L&M Software

Below is some information and questions on software distribution rights for Fenton, L&M and other software to get our heads around the idea and to get us all thinking about it.


L&M Software Status
-------------------

Paul Thacker said in an October 10, 2011 posting, "we've never talked to anyone from L&M."  L&M's program library is quite extensive.  Among the tapes is "Candy Man" one of my favorite programs on tape and one of the few games that had a sequel released on cartridge ("Ms. Candyman").

http://tinyurl.com/2cpzgbf

(or use the full URL:)

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/l&m_software/l&m_software.html

Does anyone have contact information for L&M or have reason to believe that their programs are public domain or freely distributable?


Jay Fenton Software Status
--------------------------

Paul says, "We've heard a bit from Jamie Fenton, but I don't know if the idea of public domain programs ever came up."  I bet that Jamie would gladly grant permission to have her software distributed if she were just asked.  Remember, she was the very first person to make a commercial ROM freely available for the MAME project (Robbie Roto).  Is there anyone that can contact her-- AND get a reply?


Bally BASIC and AstroBASIC Status
---------------------------------

While we're talking about it, why not bring into question distributing the AstroBASIC cart as part of the BASICart?  Even if the BASICart holds public domain software, the AstroBASIC cartridge is NOT public domain and it is half of each 8K BASICart ROM.  The status of all Astrovision software is still unknown.  Permission was given to Dave Carson in 1985 to distribute any Astrocade software-- but I have serious questions as to what this meant exactly.  Besides, it is long past 1985 and we still don't seem to know who own the rights to the majority of the software in the Astrocade's cartridge library (including its on-board ROM).  Great strides have been taken in other software communities to figure this out.  Does anyone know how it's done?  Does anyone want to seriously pursue this for us?


I would absolutely love to get some movement going on this subject.  Comments?  Ideas?

Adam

I added "How to Use the Blue Ram Basic "PLAY%( ) Command" tutorial by George Moses.  This article is from "Arcadian," June 1983, Page 128 and August 1983, Page 156.
     
This tutorial has minor revisions and corrections by Richard Degler and Adam Trionfo.  The PLAY command can be directly related to machine language programming and the Bally/Astrocade's music synthesizer (part of the I/O chip).  This article makes a perfect companion piece to the "Nutting Manual's" Music Processor section (pages 56-60) and Bally Arcade's audio information (103-105).

You can download the slightly revised document here:

http://tinyurl.com/3h33sub

(or use the full URL:)

Other versions of the document are also available including a RTF of the above version with some section breaks and bolding, the original document scans from the "Arcadian," as well as the text version of those original tutorial without revisions.  Links to these can all be found on the "Astrocade Machine Language Documentation" page, here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/ml_docs.html

I wish I understood music more.  I was able to create the terrible (and unfinished) "Happy Birthday" rendition using what I learned from this tutorial and talking with Richard Degler.  If I understood music at all, then I'm sure that I could have made the song sound like it is supposed to sound-- that is... GOOD.

Enjoy!

hardware.  All of these carts are 8K ROMs.  I'm burning them to EPROM, and I'm
(re)learning the hard way that EPROMs are temperamental beasts.  I'm using
2764s, which are 8K.  These were made about thirty years ago.  Even though they
are new old-stock, they are LONG past their life expectancy.  It is a project in
itself just to get good burns of software so that I can test it on my cart.

I've been contacting Richard with comments about the programs via email which is
working well.  He removed some of the programs that were once available in the
discussion group's file area.  These three programs were removed for copyright
reasons:

1) "Life" By Jay Fenton
2) "Nuke the Bastards" By Jay Fenton
3) "Meteoroids" By L&M Software

Below is some information and questions on software distribution rights for
Fenton, L&M and other software to get our heads around the idea and to get us
all thinking about it.

L&M Software Status
-------------------

Paul Thacker said in an October 10, 2011 posting, "we've never talked to anyone
from L&M."  L&M's program library is quite extensive.  Among the tapes is "Candy
Man" one of my favorite programs on tape and one of the few games that had a
sequel released on cartridge ("Ms. Candyman").

http://tinyurl.com/2cpzgbf

(or use the full URL:)

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/l&m_software/l&m_software.html


Does anyone have contact information for L&M or have reason to believe that
their programs are public domain or freely distributable?

Jay Fenton Software Status
--------------------------

Paul says, "We've heard a bit from Jamie Fenton, but I don't know if the idea of
public domain programs ever came up."  I bet that Jamie would gladly grant
permission to have her software distributed if she were just asked.  Remember,
she was the very first person to make a commercial ROM freely available for the
MAME project (Robbie Roto).  Is there anyone that can contact her-- AND get a
reply?

Bally BASIC and AstroBASIC Status
---------------------------------

While we're talking about it, why not bring into question distributing the
AstroBASIC cart as part of the BASICart?  Even if the BASICart holds public
domain software, the AstroBASIC cartridge is NOT public domain and it is half of
each 8K BASICart ROM.  The status of all Astrovision software is still unknown.
Permission was given to Dave Carson in 1985 to distribute any Astrocade
software-- but I have serious questions as to what this meant exactly.  Besides,
it is long past 1985 and we still don't seem to know who own the rights to the
majority of the software in the Astrocade's cartridge library (including its
on-board ROM).  Great strides have been taken in other software communities to
figure this out.  Does anyone know how it's done?  Does anyone want to seriously
pursue this for us?

I would absolutely love to get some movement going on this subject.  Comments?
Ideas?

Adam

> until Paul mentioned it, I had never even heard anyone mention that

This is one of the complications to getting permission to release
stuff...  Sometimes even the main players don't know who owns what
anymore.

> One of us writes a letter to Bally and we request the rights be
> passed into the public domain for the Bally Arcade ROMs.  I expect
> no response at all.

Calling is more likely to get a response...

> Okay, let's be optimistic.  We DO get a response that isn't a form
> letter.  It boils down to what is THAT-- we don't know what you're
> talking about.

...but just finding WHO to talk can be well nigh impossible, as you
suggest.

> So we show them hard proof that we've dug out of archives PROVING
> they own these rights.  Now, I have no idea where we'd get this
> proof, but let's suppose that we do.

That would be a big supposition, and note that articles we find
would not be PROOF.  That would take legal documents.

> Now Bally responds, "Ah.  Thanks for that info.  We've talked with
> our lawyers and they say we can not place these valuable
> intellectual properties into the public domain.  We need SOME
> <INSERT ASTRONOMICAL VALUE HERE> to sell these rights."

More likely what will happen is they'll point out that it will take
a lot of time from their legal staff and/or outside lawyers to find
and interpret all the paperwork to prove what they own, and ask US
to pay for it.

And after that, you may or may not get a reasonable rate.

> At best, that's how I see it going.  Does anyone thing otherwise?
> Is anyone more optimistic?

I've seen both sides...  I did manage to get the rights to produce
Stella Gets A New Brain, but I also ran into a lot of "we don't know",
"you'd have to pay" and "not interested" trying to get certain titles
to include.

Note however that all of my experience was toward one-time, limited
numbers, permission -- not trying to convince the company to release
all claims on their properties.

> I know that the Vectrex ROM rights were made freely distributable,
> but this was long before people even realized that these rights had
> perceived value.

I'm not sure there was no perceived value...  And note that they are
not "freely" distributable, i.e. not fully public domain -- Jay Smith
did add the caveats that they must be released at a reasonable rate,
and that Jay get a copy of the works released.  I'm sure most people
who make copies don't know this and haven't done so, but nobody is
getting rich enough even today off reproducing old Vectrex titles for
Jay to come after them.

However, I'm wondering if Jay actually owns the rights -- did they
revert to him after GCE went under?  There might still be a legal
gray area even in this example.

> Can someone point out some good and bad specific examples in this
> hobby where a company has placed these rights into the public domain
> or made them freely distributable?


I can't think of any offhand, other than Robby Roto, but I know I've
seen a few of them over the years, most likely computer titles that
were done by a person in their basement who would love to see their
games live on.  I can't think of any cases where a company put all of
their stuff in public domain...

11464:
Among the information in the Bob Fabris collection is a folder labeled "Bally D.O.S."  I flipped casually through this folder before, but today I wanted to take a closer look.  A description from the first page of the source code included in the folder reads:



"This is a CP/M compatible resident Disk Operating System.  This code is
 designed to interface into the Cromemco software system and is provided
 with an autoload feature that will load track zero, sector zero of
Drive A at RAM location 0080.  Control will then be passed to the just
loaded code at 0080."


Here is a list of the documentation included in the folder:


1) Personal letter to Bob Fabris from Stu Haigh, the author of the DOS.  The complete letter is transcribed below.

2) "Arcadian RDOS 1.0" source code, 33 pages

3) "Arcadian RDOS 1.0" Listing (Intel hex format), 4 Pages

4) Western Digital FD1771 Floppy Disk Formatter/Controller Datasheet (June 9, 1978)(poor photocopy), 12 Pages

5) Western Digital FD1771 A/B - 01 and 02 Floppy Disk Formatter/Controller Datasheet (1977)(Very poor photocopy), 24 Pages

6) "TMS 5501 I/O Controller in TMS 8080A Microprocessor System" Article by Engineering Staff of Texas Instruments Inc., 16 Pages


The personal letter to Bob from Stu is short and so I've included it here:


Bob,

This code uses a 5501 as a com. ctrler and a 1771 Flex Disk ctrl.  It will support four 5 1/4 inch, or 2 5 1/4 & 1-9, or 2-9 inch Disk Drives.

I have ALL of the documentation, that is a user's manual.  I can let you have a copy, limited, of the code burned into 2716's if you want to try it out.  I didn't get around to copying the "manual" but if you want it just drop a line or call.

P.S.  Can also ReORG and Burn for any location other than 0C00h.


No DOS manual is included in the folder or elsewhere (that I've found so far), so I guess that Bob didn't ask Stu for it.  I also didn't see the DOS software burned onto any of the ROMs that were part of the Bob Fabris Collection.  I was going to scan the source, but it's not easy to scan and I can't imagine who could possibly use it.  Stu doesn't give exact details on which Cromemco controller that he uses.  Even if he DID give that information I have no idea how it would interface with a Bally/Astrocade.  I can't find the exact reference, but I suppose that this is the DOS that Bob Fabris is referring to in the Arcadian when he says that someone is working on a Disk Operating System.  Also, of note, is that the Z-Grass unit uses the Western Digital 1770 series disk controller too.

It's clear that some people WANTED a disk drive for the Astrocade.  People WANTED that Bally Arcade game console to be a full-fledged computer system.  At least one person wanted it so badly that he went ahead and did it himself!

My CP/M experience is extremely limited.  The only time I used it with real hardware was with a Commodore 128 and a Commodore 1571 disk drive-- hardly a typical old-school CP/M system.  Has anyone here used one of the Cromemco disk controllers before on a CP/M system?

Adam

>>
Would someone please give me step by step instructions on how to  emulate astrocade on my PC ( windows xp ). specifically BALLY BASIC!
>>

That's a tall order.  I'm not aware of any that exist.  Getting MESS to work can seem involved or complicated depending on your computer experience and previous use of emulators.  Here are the basic steps:

1) Download the latest version of MESS, here:

http://www.mess.org/downloads

The most recent version Windows version is MESS 0.143.  A direct link to this archive is here:

http://www.mess.org/_media/downloads:mess0143b.zip


2) Next you want to download the Bally/Astrocade and Arcade ROMs, here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/emulation/cart_images/cart_images.html

The most recent archive is from September.  A direct link is here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/emulation/cart_images/ROMs/astrocade_rom_collection_9-30-2011.zip


3) Unarchive and install MESS.


4) In the mess0143b directory create another directory called:

ROMs\astrocde


5) Place astro.bin from the software archive (downloaded in step 2) into:

mess0143b\ROMs\astrocde


6) In the mess0143b directory create another directory called:

software\astrocde


7) In the mess0143b\software\astrocde directory place the Astrocade cartridges that you want to play.  We'll try AstroBASIC, so place the file called astrobas.bin into:

mess0143b\software\astrocde


8) MESS can be started in a number of ways.  As a new user, to make it simple, I'll say just double-click the file messui.exe

9) MESS will start and you'll be presented with hundreds of different systems to emulate.  Work your way down to Bally Professional Arcade and double-click it.  This will start the Astrocade emulator as if no cartridge was installed.  The main menu will display Gunfight, Checkmate, Calculator and Scribbling.  If that works, then continue.  If not, then you may get a number of different errors.  Try backing up and reviewing the previous steps.  If that doesn't help, then ask for help on this discussion board and be sure to include any error messages that appear.

10)  Once you've emulated the Astrocade you can press escape to return to the MESS GUI.  The idea here is to try AstroBASIC.  In the MESS GUI, to the right of the systems are several tabs.  The tab highlighted by default is called "Software."  Under that is one ROM called Astrobas.bin.  Double-click Astrobas.bin and AstroBASIC will start.


If you get AstroBASIC to start, then the next step is to configure the keys in an easy-to-use fashion-- which can take awhile (default setup of MESS is not AstroBASIC friendly).  If you get as far as AstroBASIC starting, then say so and I'll help you configure the keyboard.  In the meantime, you can try any games by placing them into the mess0143b\software\astrocde folder.  The default keys for Hand Controller # 1 are arrow keys and control.

Anyone else who has wanted to emulate the Astrocade but hasn't done so should try following along with us.

Adam

The most recent version Windows version is MESS 0.143.  A direct link to this archive is here:

http://www.mess.org/_media/downloads:mess0143b.zip

2) Next you want to download the Bally/Astrocade and Arcade ROMs, here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/emulation/cart_images/cart_images.html

The most recent archive is from September.  A direct link is here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/emulation/cart_images/ROMs/astrocade_rom_collection_9-30-2011.zip

3) Unarchive and install MESS.

4) In the mess0143b directory create another directory called:

ROMs\astrocde

5) Place astro.bin from the software archive (downloaded in step 2) into:

mess0143b\ROMs\astrocde

6) In the mess0143b directory create another directory called:

software\astrocde

7) In the mess0143b\software\astrocde directory place the Astrocade cartridges that you want to play.  We'll try AstroBASIC, so place the file called astrobas.bin into:

mess0143b\software\astrocde

start, then the next step is to configure the keys in an easy-to-use fashion-- which can take awhile (default setup of MESS is not AstroBASIC friendly).  If you get as far as AstroBASIC starting, then say so and I'll help you configure the keyboard.  In the meantime, you can try any games by placing them into the mess0143b\software\astrocde folder.  The default keys for Hand Controller # 1 are arrow keys and control.

Great to hear it!
 
Next up is configuring the keypad for input.  The idea is to configure your keyboard to emulate the Astrocade keypad overlay as closely as possible:


http://tinyurl.com/7lfx3f3

or use the full URL:

http://www.ballyalley.com/pics/keypad_overlays/full_size/AstroBASIC%20Overlay%20%28150%20dpi%29.jpg
 
 
If you have a spare keyboard, then I HIGHLY recommend the approach that I took.  Check out the emulation section, here:
 
http://www.ballyalley.com/emulation/MESS/mess.html
 
Scroll down to the part labeled "Astrocade MESS Keyboard Labels/Stickers."
 
If you don't have a spare keyboard, then I suggest that you get one, as I never could find a good approach mapping the keys.
 
Here is how to actually change the keyboard mapping:
 
1) While MESS is running, press Tab.
 
2) Choose "Input (This System)"
 
3) Go down to each key that needs to be mapped and press the Delete key.  This makes the input for that key be "None."
 
4) Now go to each key and change to the mapping that you desire by pressing "Enter" and then the key that you want to use for Astrocade input.
 
As an example of getting the keyboard mapping started for the way that I have MESS setup with my keyboard stickers:
 
1) Start MESS.
2) Press TAB.
3) Choose "Input (This System)"
4) Highlight the first selection, which is "CH 9 GHI STEP."
5) Press "Delete."  The input for that selection becomes "None."
6) Press "Enter."
7) Press "W."  The keyboard mapping for "CH 9 GHI STEP" is now "W."
8) Now choose the next selection, which is "% [Divide Sign] [Empty] LIST."
9) Press "1."
10) Continue this for the rest of the 24 keys.

This takes a little while, but it only has to be done once.  Note that this only changes the keyboard mapping for the current system ROM.  Since there are three of them, you could technically had a different keyboard mapping for each system if you wanted to do that.

Enjoy!

Adam

I added a disassembly of the "The Incredible Wizard" for the Bally/Astrocade.  This is the popular "Wizard of Wor" clone.  Everybody who is an Astrocade fan is aware of this game, and for good reason: it's great.
    
I've put about twenty-five hours into disassembling this game so far (starting at the beginning of November).  There is a lot of work that needs to be done, but this is a solid beginning.   I need to set it aside for now (probably for at least a few weeks-- maybe more), but I figured it would be a good idea to share what I've done so far as I see no reason that it needs to lay about on my hard drive where no one else can access it.

You can download the disassembly of "The Incredible Wizard" here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_source/wizwor.asm

Some general notes about the disassembly:

1)  This source code assembles using ZMac into an 8K byte-for-byte copy of the ROM cartridge.

2)  This program doesn't appear to use On-Board ROM vector routines for graphics.  If it does, then I have not been able to find where they begin.  More likely is that for speed this game uses its own routines.

3)  I did find quite a bit of the graphics and have identified them.  Even non-coders can wade through the code and check-out most of the graphics to the game.

4)  I never noticed this before I began disassembling the game, but "Incredible Wizard" only uses four colors!

5)  The sound effects don't seem to use the on-board music routines-- or I couldn't find them.

6)  I never did find the drawing routines for the levels-- which was one of the primary reason that I started the disassembly in the first place.

7)  Finally, even on the "easy" level, that Wizard is FAST!  When or why does he appear?  Does he appear at random?

This disassembly could not have been completed to this point without Richard Degler's disassembly script for the DZ80 disassember.  I HIGHLY encourage those that understand ML it give it a whirl.  It works fantastic and will save you a TON of work!

Enjoy!

Adam

Today I was looking though the Bob Fabris collection.  I was looking for the Bally Service Manual (which I DID find).  Of course, the Service Manual was in the very last box (of about eight boxes) that I looked in.  As I was looking through all the boxes I got a sickening feeling.  What if it was all destroyed in some manner?  You can choose the manner it could happen-- they all went through my mind (fire, theft, flood, etc.).  There are items in there that just are NOT replaceable.

What is the best and most efficient manner to archive this material?  Should I pick a box and start scanning everything until it is all done and THEN choose another box, scan that one, and so on for several months?  To save time, it might be better to scan it all in grayscale, rather than try to make the files small for download.  Once everything is scanned I could THEN sort through the massive amounts of material.  Scanning and saving as TIFF would take time, but at least there would be a goal in sight.  When everything is done I could send out five or six DVDs to several individuals so that I'm not the ONLY person that has all of this paperwork.

Does this make sense?  Is there a better method?

Adam

For the last few years, historian and archivist Jason Scott has been involved with a loose, rogue band of data preservation activists called The Archive Team.  As major sites with brand recognition and the work of millions announce short-notice shutdowns of their entire services, including Geocities, Friendster, and Yahoo Video, Archive Team arrives on the scene to duplicate as much as they possibly can for history before all the data is wiped forever.  To do this, they have been rude, crude and far outside the spectrum of polite requests to save digital history, and have used a variety of techniques to retrieve and extract data that might have otherwise been unreachable.  Come for the rough-and-tumble extraction techniques and teamwork methods, stay for the humor and ranting.

I added two versions of the Bally "Football" source code to BallyAlley.com.

I combined two previous scanned pdf files of the Bally "Football" cartridge source code into one pdf file for easier use.  This version of the pdf can be downloaded here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_source/Football%20(Source).pdf


I have retyped the source code for Bally "Football."  It can be easily assembled with the ZMac assembler and the final ROM matches byte-for-byte with the original released cartridge.  The assembly source code file can be downloaded here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_source/football.asm


Note that the available original source code had a few differences with the final version.  I have changed the source file so that it produces the cartridge version, as the available scanned source code was obviously not the final shipped product (but it was very close).

This source code exhausts the very limited availability of original source code.  I have no more to scan.  The only ML source code that has been scanned but NOT made into a text version that can be assembled is "Star Battle."  That source code is actually a disassembly by Tom Woods from 1979-- and it is mostly uncommented.  If you have any original source code that needs to be scanned, then send it my way and I'll get it up on the Bally Alley website.

Have fun!

11495:
Added "Fast Action Graphics" which is probably by John Perkins.  This program is from an article in the "Arcadian" Vol 2, No. 10 (Sept 17. 1980)

"Fast Action Graphics" using Foreground/Background Processing.  This program runs on a Bally/Astrocade in the expansion RAM beginning at $6000.  This program was originally meant to be entered into the Blue Ram Utility as a machine language program.

Watch the Perkin's Engineering graphic (a "PE") bounce around the screen without disturbing what is there!  The speed of motion is controlled by the #1 knob.  Another special effect produced by this routine is a "curtain of invisibility" at the top of the screen.  As the graphic moves behind the curtain, it disappears one-half pixel at a time.  The size of the curtain is also controlled by the #1 knob.  Notice that you can still enter programs, etc. in BASIC because the graphic movement is performed in the background mode where it does not tie up the processor.

The source code for "Fast Action Graphics" can be downloaded here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_homebrew/fastactn.asm

Enjoy!

Adam

I updated Brett Bilbrey's "Critter" source code so that it runs under AstroBASIC.  A version of this source code was already added to BallyAlley.com, but I made some minor tweaks and uploaded this to the homebrew area, rather than to just have it included with the "Critter 2000!" article.

This Z80 source is based on what appears in the "PEEK N' POKE manual."  It been changed so that it runs under AstroBASIC and assembles under Zmac.  The Z80 code it generates is the same as the BASIC listings that appear in the Arcadian and the Cursor newsletters except that the interrupt routine location has been changed from the Bally BASIC routine to the AstroBASIC routine.

When assembled this program will NOT run as a cartridge as the program is meant to be run in AstroBASIC.  The BASIC version of "Critter" can be found after the source code at the end of this file.

Have fun!

11498:
I added a "Hello World ML Tutorial" that I wrote.  I was going to eventually create a nicely formatted html article with link and pictures, but I suspect that isn't going to happen anytime soon.  I figure that I can always revise the tutorial later, so why not get the real meat of it online right now.

This tutorial describes how to get a "Hello World" program running on a Bally Arcade / Astrocade.  This article is aimed at those who want to get started programming the Astrocade using an assembler.

For those people playing with classic systems, the words "assembler" and "assembly language" are thrown around rather often with little or no explanation of what the words mean.  If you're just playing cartridges on your Bally/Astrocade, or loading a few BASIC programs, then there is no reason to understand how the game cartridges work.  However, if the idea of what is going on DOES interest you, then this article will benefit you.  After you finish reading, you will not only have a better understanding of an assembler, but you will also know how to use one.
     
You an read the "'HELLO, WORLD!' ML Tutorial" here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/hello_world/Hello_World_ML_Tutorial.txt

Enjoy!

Adam
